Optimizers · from SGD to Adam

From SGD to Adam, one fix at a time

Each optimizer here fixes one specific failure of the one before it. We build them in the order the ideas were found, and watch each fix, and each new failure, happen.

How to use this deck

  • Press Enter to reveal the next piece of a slide. The dots at the bottom centre show how many steps the slide has.
  • Some slides have sliders. Drag them, then press Enter again to continue: the keyboard goes back to the deck when you release the mouse.

The story in one paragraph

SGD uses one learning rate for every parameter, and the steepest direction forces it to be small. Newton would fix this with curvature, but the Hessian is far too big. So we look for a cheap per-parameter number to divide by. Rprop uses only the sign, which breaks on noisy minibatches. AdaGrad divides by the accumulated gradient size, which never stops growing. RMSProp divides by a moving average instead. Adam adds momentum and fixes the start-up bias.

01 · Vanilla SGD

SGD: step against the minibatch gradient

is the learning rate: one scalar, shared by every parameter.

Why −g? A first-order Taylor expansion

Near :

Among all steps of the same length, lowers this linear model the most: .

The expansion says which way, not how far

The linear model keeps promising more the farther you go. All of "how far" is packed into .

Toy loss L = ½(x² + 4y²) at θ = (1.4, 0.9); the slice is L along the −g direction.

Explain

  • Step 1: the point θ and its gradient g. The gradient points uphill, so we step along −g.
  • Step 2: the ring shows many candidate steps of the same length, coloured by how much the linear model says each one lowers the loss (blue: down, coral: up, grey: flat). The best one is exactly −g. That is all the Taylor expansion gives you: a direction.
  • Step 3: walk along −g and plot the real loss. The linear model (straight line) keeps going down forever; the real loss is a parabola that turns back up.
  • Step 4: so the step length is a separate decision. η = 0.05 barely moves, η ≈ 0.28 lands near the bottom of the slice, η = 0.65 ends higher than it started.

Check yourself

  • Why can't the first-order expansion tell you the right η? It is linear: it has no curvature term, so it never predicts that the loss turns back up.

01 · Vanilla SGD · Units

A units check: what η would have to be

Give each parameter a unit (metres, say). The update only makes sense if is also in .

One scalar η can't be right for everyone

It works for all parameters at once only if they share the same scale and curvature. In a network they don't: embeddings, biases and the weights of different layers can have gradients that differ by orders of magnitude.

Same model, new units: SGD changes its mind

Rewrite one parameter as . The gradient becomes , SGD moves by , so itself moves times less.

Explain

  • Treat each parameter as a physical quantity with a unit. The loss has its own unit. A derivative divides by the parameter's unit, so the gradient is "loss per metre".
  • For θ − η·g to be "metres minus metres", η must carry metres² per loss. That unit is different for every parameter, so one shared number can only be right for all of them by coincidence.
  • The chart makes it concrete: k = 1000 means measuring the same parameter in millimetres instead of metres. Nothing about the model changed, yet SGD now moves it a million times less.
  • The dashed line is what we want: a step that does not care about units. Keep it in mind; RMSProp gets there (section 06).

Check yourself

  • If you halve a parameter's scale (k = 0.5), how does SGD's actual move change? It grows 4×: the move scales like 1/k².

02 · The ill-conditioned valley

The simplest hard case: a long, narrow valley

Steep walls along , a nearly flat floor along . Here , .

The gradient points across the valley

. The steep coordinate dominates, so points mostly at the opposite wall, not down the valley toward the minimum.

Each coordinate is its own 1-D problem

Every step multiplies each coordinate by its own factor.

SGD with η = 0.09

Just under . Along the factor is : it flips side every step. Along it is : only 9% closer per step.

Explain

  • This quadratic is the local picture of almost any smooth loss near a minimum, after rotating to the Hessian's eigenvectors. a and b are the curvatures (eigenvalues).
  • Because the axes are not coupled, the gradient's x part only depends on x and its y part only on y. So SGD runs two independent 1-D iterations with the same η.
  • The arrows: at the marked point the gradient is (20·x, y) = (−6, 1.1). Its x part is 5× bigger, so the step goes mostly sideways.

Check yourself

  • What is the per-step factor along y if η = 0.09 and b = 1? 1 − 0.09 = 0.91.

02 · The ill-conditioned valley · Stability

The steep direction sets the speed limit: η < 2/a

Along , every step multiplies the distance to the minimum by . Four values of , on the parabola :

Explain

  • One coordinate, one multiplier r = 1 − ηa per step. After t steps the distance is rᵗ times the start.
  • |r| < 1 shrinks, |r| > 1 grows. A negative r means each step jumps over the minimum to the other side.
  • ηa = 1 lands exactly on the minimum: that is the 1-D Newton step, η = 1/a (section 03).
  • So the steepest curvature a caps the learning rate at 2/a, for every parameter.

Check yourself

  • With a = 60, what is the largest stable η? 2/60 ≈ 0.033.

to cut the distance 1000×, at the best single η

The core pathology

One learning rate has to be small enough for the steepest direction, and is therefore far too small for the flattest one.

Curves use the best single learning rate η = 2/(a+b): both coordinates then shrink by (κ−1)/(κ+1) per step. Left: κ = 20, same η.

Explain

  • To keep x stable, η < 2/a. Plug that into y's factor: 1 − ηb > 1 − 2b/a = 1 − 2/κ. So each step removes at most about 2/κ of y's distance.
  • Shrinking by (1 − 2/κ) per step takes about κ/2 steps per factor of e. Cutting the distance 1000× (≈ 6.9 factors of e) takes ≈ 3.5κ steps: 35, 346, 3,454.
  • The best single η is 2/(a+b), which balances the two directions: x shrinks by −(κ−1)/(κ+1), y by +(κ−1)/(κ+1). Even that optimum is ≈ 1 − 2/κ. No η beats it.
  • Real networks have κ in the thousands or more, across millions of directions.

Check yourself

  • Doubling κ roughly does what to the number of steps? Doubles it.

03 · The fix we'd want

The ideal: a step size per direction, set by curvature

Newton divides each gradient by its curvature.

One step to the minimum, whatever κ is

Dividing by and undoes the stretch of the valley: the step is exactly .

Out of reach for a network

has entries. With parameters that is numbers, about 40 PB in float32, before you even invert it.

The affordable proxy

Find a cheap per-parameter number that is large where the gradient is large, and divide by it:

The obvious candidate: the gradient's own size

Rprop, AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam differ mainly in how they estimate .

Explain

  • Newton's step comes from the second-order Taylor model L(θ+Δ) ≈ L + gᵀΔ + ½ΔᵀHΔ. Minimising it gives Δ = −H⁻¹g. The curvature term is exactly what the first-order model was missing on slide 2.
  • On the quadratic, the second-order model is exact, so one Newton step lands on the minimum.
  • For a network: storing H is n², inverting it is about n³. Even the diagonal of H is not free to compute exactly. So we want something we get almost for free from the gradients we already have.
  • Why the gradient's size is a sensible proxy: where the loss is steep, gradients are big, and those are exactly the directions that need smaller steps.

Check yourself

  • Newton divides x's gradient by a. What would dividing by |g_x| = a|x| give instead? A step of size η in x, whatever a is. We come back to this difference in section 06.

03 · The fix we'd want · Preview

Preview: divide by the gradient's size, and κ stops mattering

SGDRMSProp (β = 0.9)start (−1.5, 1) · minimum at the centre

SGD zigzags along the steep axis and crawls along the flat one. Push its learning rate past and it diverges.

RMSProp heads almost diagonally to the minimum but never settles on it: it ends up bouncing at about the scale of its learning rate.

SGD final loss
RMSProp final loss

Both behaviours fall straight out of the math in the next sections.

Things to try

  • Raise a to 200. SGD's learning rate now has to be below 0.01 or it diverges, and at 0.01 it barely moves along y. RMSProp's path hardly changes.
  • Set SGD's learning rate just above the 2/a line: the zigzag grows instead of shrinking.
  • Raise steps to 300 and watch RMSProp's loss curve: it first plunges far below SGD, then jumps back up and stays flat. That flat part is the bounce between two points about η/2 from the minimum.

Why the plunge, then the bounce?

On this noise-free valley, RMSProp's moving average v lags behind the shrinking gradient, so for a while the steps shrink faster than the distance and it converges very fast. But v keeps decaying by β every step. Once √v catches up with the tiny gradient, the step is back to ≈ η and the iterate hops over the minimum. With minibatch noise, that bounce is there from the start.

Check yourself

  • Why does RMSProp's path start out on a 45° diagonal? Its first steps move x and y by the same amount, whatever their gradients: the gradient's size is divided out.

04 · Stepping stones · Rprop

Rprop: keep only the sign, and a step size per parameter

Riedmiller & Braun, 1993. The gradient's magnitude is thrown away entirely.

Full batch, it works

Rprop (amber) accelerates along the flat floor while the sign repeats, and brakes on the steep wall each time the sign flips. SGD at its best shown faint.

Scale-free: immune to κ

. Drag the slider: the contours and SGD's path change, Rprop's path does not move at all.

Simplest Rprop variant (no step backtracking): Δ starts at 0.1, capped to [10⁻⁶, 1]. 30 steps from (−1.2, 1).

Explain

  • Each parameter keeps its own step length Δᵢ. The gradient only decides the direction: sign(gᵢ).
  • While the sign keeps repeating, you are clearly still far from the bottom in that coordinate, so Δᵢ grows by 20% per step. When the sign flips, you just jumped over the bottom, so Δᵢ halves.
  • Because the size of the gradient never enters, the stretch a of the valley cannot matter. This is the per-direction step size we wanted from Newton, learned by trial and error.

Check yourself

  • What happens to Δ along the flat y axis over the first five steps? It grows 1.2× per step: 0.1, 0.12, 0.144, 0.173, 0.207.

04 · Stepping stones · Rprop's failure

…but on minibatches, signs can't average out

Hinton's example: a weight gets on nine minibatches and on the tenth. The average gradient is zero, so the weight should stay put.

Magnitude is what lets noise cancel

SGD sums the magnitudes, so +0.9 and −0.9 cancel every cycle. The sign rule moves nine steps one way and one step back: a steady drift.

Step size η = 0.01 for both; positions in units of η. Sign rule with a fixed step shown; Rprop's growing Δ drifts about 5× faster still.

Explain

  • Minibatch gradients are noisy samples of the true gradient. Here the samples are +0.1, +0.1, … , −0.9, which average to exactly zero.
  • SGD: the position is −η times the running sum of gradients. Over each cycle the sum returns to zero, so the weight just wiggles by 0.9η around its start.
  • Sign only: nine steps of −η and one step of +η per cycle, so −8η per cycle, forever. The −0.9 carried the information "this is big", and the sign threw it away.
  • Full Rprop is worse: during the nine same-sign steps Δ grows by 1.2 each time. In our simulation it drifted about 5× further than the fixed-step sign rule.

Check yourself

  • Why does Rprop work full-batch but not here? Full-batch gradients are exact, so their sign is trustworthy. Minibatch signs are noisy, and only magnitudes can average the noise away.

04 · Stepping stones · AdaGrad

AdaGrad: keep the magnitude, divide by the whole history

Duchi et al., 2011. All operations are elementwise: one per parameter.

Great for sparse features

A frequent parameter gets a gradient every step, a rare one every 10th step. The rare one's grows 10× slower, so it keeps larger steps.

But only ever grows

Constant gradient 1 for 200 steps, then the landscape flattens (gradient 0.1) and the weight still needs to move. AdaGrad's step has already decayed like .

The flaw: the effective learning rate decays roughly like and eventually stalls, even when the landscape has changed and you need to move.

Explain

  • AdaGrad keeps the magnitude (fixing Rprop's minibatch problem) and divides by √G, the root of the summed squared gradients. Parameters that have seen big gradients get small steps.
  • Sparse features (rare words, rare categories) get gradients only now and then. Their G stays small, so when a gradient does arrive they take a big step. This is why AdaGrad was popular for NLP and click-through models.
  • The problem: G is a sum, so it never shrinks. With a steady gradient, G = t·g², and the step is η/√t. At t = 10,000 the step is 1% of the first one.
  • In the right chart, after step 200 the gradient drops to 0.1. The step drops to about 0.007η and keeps shrinking: AdaGrad has "used up" its learning rate.

Check yourself

  • With a constant gradient, what is AdaGrad's step at t = 100, relative to the first? 1/√100 = 10%.

05 · RMSProp

RMSProp: replace the sum with a moving average

Weight on each past

β

is the root mean square of the recent gradients: hence RMS-Prop. Hinton, 2012 Coursera lecture, never formally published.

Same test as AdaGrad: the step recovers

Explain

  • One change to AdaGrad: instead of adding every g², keep an exponential moving average (EMA). Old gradients fade by β per step.
  • Unrolled: v_t = (1−β)·Σ βᵏ·g²_{t−k}. The weights (1−β)βᵏ add up to 1, so v_t is an average, not a sum. It estimates E[g²] over roughly the last 1/(1−β) steps: 10 for β = 0.9, 100 for β = 0.99.
  • Because it is an average, √v tracks the current scale of the gradient. When the landscape flattens at step 200, √v follows the gradient down within a few dozen steps and the step returns to ≈ η.
  • Notice the first step in the right chart: about 3.2η, not η. That is the v₀ = 0 start-up bias, covered in section 07.

Check yourself

  • What fraction of v's weight sits on the last 10 gradients when β = 0.9? 1 − 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 65%.

05 · RMSProp · Minibatches

"The minibatch version of Rprop"

Consecutive minibatches are divided by nearly the same number, so their magnitudes still add up and cancel. Only the overall scale is normalised away, much like Rprop's sign.

Drift per 10-step cycle

0
SGD
−8η
sign
−0.07η
RMSProp

RMSProp with β = 0.99 and v₀ set to the true mean square (0.09), to separate this effect from the start-up bias of section 07. With β = 0.9 the drift is ≈ 0.7η per cycle: still 12× less than the sign rule.

Explain

  • Hinton's framing: Rprop is great but only full-batch. RMSProp is the version that works on minibatches.
  • Why it works: within a cycle, √v ≈ 0.3 (bottom strip) changes only a little, so +0.1 steps become ≈ +0.33η and the −0.9 step becomes ≈ −3η. They still add up to about zero, like SGD's.
  • Why it is not exactly zero: the −0.9 step is taken right after v absorbs 0.81, so it is divided by a slightly larger number than the +0.1 steps. A longer window (bigger β) means a steadier √v and less drift.
  • And like Rprop, the overall scale is gone: multiply every gradient by 100 and RMSProp's path is unchanged, while SGD's wiggles grow 100×.

Check yourself

  • What would RMSProp do if v were frozen at a constant? It would be exactly SGD with learning rate η/√v, so the cycle would cancel exactly.

06 · Why it works · View 1 of 3

Normalisation: η becomes a distance

The ratio has no units. Scale a parameter's gradients by 1000 and numerator and denominator both grow 1000×: the step is unchanged. So now has the units of the parameter itself.

Multiply one parameter's gradients by k

η means "how far to move per step"

On the valley, and its RMS is about , so each step moves by about , whatever is. Same for . That is the diagonal path.

…which is also why it jitters

With a constant the step never shrinks to zero, so the iterate ends up hopping over the minimum. In practice: pair RMSProp with a learning-rate decay.

Explain

  • Units check again: g is "loss per metre", RMS(g) is also "loss per metre", so g/RMS(g) is a pure number around ±1. Multiply by η and you get metres: η is now a distance in parameter space.
  • That is what makes one η usable across layers with wildly different gradient scales, and it is the "step that does not care about units" we wanted on slide 3.
  • The valley: the first steps move x and y by the same amount (they are even 3.2× too big at the start, from v₀ = 0). Equal steps in x and y means a 45° path.
  • The bottom chart is |x| over time for a = 60. With constant η = 0.1, x plunges, then settles into hopping between ±η/2 = ±0.05. With η_t = η/(1 + t/20), the hop shrinks with η_t.

Check yourself

  • If η = 0.001 and a weight is 0.05, roughly how many steps can it take to move by its own size? About 50: the step is ≈ η regardless of the gradient's scale.

06 · Why it works · View 2 of 3

Signal-to-noise: small steps where minibatches disagree

Split one coordinate's minibatch gradient into its mean (signal) and spread (noise). measures both together.

Consistent gradient (σ ≪ μ)

The step is about : full speed.

Mostly noise (σ ≫ μ)

The step shrinks toward : RMSProp automatically goes carefully.

Hollow dot: a live simulation of RMSProp's mean step on a stream g ~ N(μ, σ²), β = 0.99, 6,000 steps.

Explain

  • E[g²] = Var(g) + E[g]² = σ² + μ². So √v is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs μ and σ.
  • On average the numerator g contributes μ; the denominator is that hypotenuse. Their ratio is the cosine of the angle: 1 when there is no noise, small when the noise leg dominates.
  • Near a minimum, the true gradient μ gets small while minibatch noise σ stays. So RMSProp's steps shrink on their own as you approach the bottom, even with a constant η. (Not to zero, though: the bounce on the last slide.)
  • Drag the slider and compare the hollow dot (simulation) with the curve (formula). They agree within a few percent.

Check yourself

  • σ = μ: how big is the step? η/√2 ≈ 0.71η.

06 · Why it works · View 3 of 3

Curvature, with a caveat: a sign method in disguise

estimates the diagonal of , the empirical Fisher, so RMSProp is often described as a cheap diagonal Newton or natural-gradient step. On the quadratic that link is loose:

Newton divides by curvature

: the step is proportional to the distance, and cancels.

SGD divides by nothing

: the slope of this line is , so it swings with the curvature.

RMSProp divides by curvature × distance

, so : flat in both and distance.

A smart sign method

Not curvature alone. Kunstner et al. (2019) is a good read on where the empirical-Fisher view breaks down.

η = 0.02 for SGD and 0.1 for RMSProp (steady state, √v ≈ |g|). Kunstner, Balles & Hennig, "Limitations of the empirical Fisher approximation for natural gradient descent", NeurIPS 2019.

Explain

  • The Fisher matrix is E[∇log p ∇log pᵀ] under the model's own predictions. The "empirical" Fisher uses the observed labels instead, which is just E[g gᵀ] over minibatches. Its diagonal is exactly what v estimates.
  • For some losses, near a minimum, the Fisher matches the Hessian. That is the source of the "RMSProp ≈ diagonal Newton" story.
  • But on a quadratic without noise, g = a·x, so √v ≈ a·|x|. Dividing by it removes the curvature and the distance. Newton only removes the curvature, so Newton's step shrinks as you approach the minimum and RMSProp's doesn't.
  • That is the third angle on the jitter: Newton would slow down near the bottom; RMSProp keeps stepping ≈ η.

Check yourself

  • Which of the three lines would be unchanged if you measured x in millimetres? RMSProp's step in its own units is always ≈ η; Newton's step is exact in any units; SGD's slope changes by k².

07 · Knobs and pitfalls · Decay rate

β trades responsiveness against noise

is an estimate of the gradient's current scale. Below, the true scale jumps from 1 to 4 at step 150 and back at step 350.

Keras

RMSprop(learning_rate=0.001, rho=0.9)

PyTorch

RMSprop(lr=0.01, alpha=0.99)

Same word, new meaning

"Learning rate" here is a step size in parameter units, not SGD's .

Explain

  • The window is about 1/(1−β) steps. β = 0.9 reacts to the jump within ~10 steps but its estimate is noisy: a few large gradients move it a lot. β = 0.99 is smooth but needs ~100 steps to catch up, and during that lag the step size is wrong.
  • Too-small √v after a jump (β = 0.99 at step 150–250) means steps that are too big: a common source of loss spikes when the gradient scale suddenly grows.
  • Defaults differ between libraries, and so does the learning rate's meaning compared with SGD: values that are good for SGD are usually wrong for RMSProp and vice versa.

Check yourself

  • Your gradients change scale every ~20 steps. β = 0.9 or 0.999? 0.9: a 1,000-step window would average across many regimes.

07 · Knobs and pitfalls · Epsilon

ε guards the division, and also caps the step

For parameters whose gradients are much smaller than , RMSProp degrades into SGD with learning rate .

Above ε: normalised

The step is about , however small the gradient. A gradient of still moves the weight a full step.

Below ε: SGD-like

The step is , proportional to the gradient. So sets the scale below which a gradient counts as "nothing".

Larger ε on purpose

Values from to are sometimes chosen deliberately to damp full-size steps on tiny, noisy gradients.

Steady gradient assumed, so √v = |g|. PyTorch's default ε is 10⁻⁸, Keras's 10⁻⁷.

Explain

  • ε exists so the division is safe when v = 0, for example a parameter that has never received a gradient.
  • Side effect: with a steady gradient, the step is η·|g|/(|g| + ε). Above ε it saturates at η. Below ε it is (η/ε)·|g|, which is just SGD with a (huge) learning rate η/ε.
  • With ε = 10⁻⁸, even a 10⁻⁷ gradient gets an almost full step. If that gradient is pure noise, you are taking full-size random steps. A larger ε treats such gradients as negligible.

Check yourself

  • η = 10⁻³ and ε = 10⁻⁸: what SGD learning rate does RMSProp turn into for very tiny gradients? η/ε = 10⁵.

07 · Knobs and pitfalls · Initialisation

Starting from v₀ = 0 inflates the first steps

The first estimate is far below the true , so the first step is too big. With a steady gradient, step is times too big.

Tolerable at 0.9 and 0.99

A few big early steps, then it settles.

A real problem at 0.999

A 30× first step, and steps more than 10% too big for over a thousand steps.

Exactly why Adam adds bias correction

Divide by and every step, from the first, is the right size. Derived in section 08.

"Gone" = the step is less than 1.1× its steady size. Constant gradient, ε ignored.

Explain

  • v starts at 0 and only gets (1−β) of each new g². After one step it holds 10% of g² (β = 0.9), so √v is 32% of |g| and the step is 1/0.316 = 3.2× too big.
  • With a constant gradient, v_t = (1 − βᵗ)·g² exactly, so the step is 1/√(1 − βᵗ) too big. That factor dies out over about 1/(1−β) steps.
  • Adam wants β₂ = 0.999 for a stable scale estimate. Without a fix, that would mean a ×31.6 first step. Hence the correction.

Check yourself

  • Why does the RMSProp chart on slide 12 start at about 3.2? β = 0.9, so the first step is 1/√0.1 ≈ 3.2× too big.

07 · Knobs and pitfalls · Variants

Two variants: centred RMSProp, and momentum

centered=True

is a variance, so this divides by a standard deviation instead of an RMS: the step becomes the signal-to-noise ratio itself.

With momentum

PyTorch's momentum= option: a velocity built from the normalised steps.

That last idea is where Adam comes in

Adam is essentially RMSProp's denominator, plus a moving average of the gradient itself as the numerator (momentum), plus bias correction for both averages. Once RMSProp makes sense, Adam is roughly a 3-line diff.

Explain

  • Plain RMSProp divides by √E[g²] = √(μ² + σ²). Centred RMSProp subtracts the squared mean, leaving √σ² = σ. So the expected step is η·μ/σ.
  • On the chart: plain RMSProp's step saturates at η when the gradient is consistent; centred keeps growing with μ/σ. That sharpens the signal-to-noise reading, at the price of possibly large steps when σ is tiny (ε then matters more).
  • Momentum: accumulate the normalised steps in a velocity b. Directions where the normalised step keeps its sign build up speed; directions where it flips cancel.

Check yourself

  • For a perfectly constant gradient, what does centred RMSProp's denominator approach? ε: the variance is zero. So ε caps the step there.

08 · Adam · The diff

Adam = RMSProp + momentum + bias correction

Keep RMSProp's denominator. Add a moving average of the gradient as the numerator. Correct both averages for starting at zero.

  # one step, per parameter, t = 1, 2, …
v = β2·v + (1 − β2)·g²       # RMSProp's scalem = β1·m + (1 − β1)·g        # momentum: EMA of gm̂ = m / (1 − β1ᵗ)            # bias correctionsv̂ = v / (1 − β2ᵗ)θ = θ − η·g / (√v + ε)θ = θ − α·m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)       # the update

Numerator: momentum

Parts of the gradient that flip sign cancel in ; the consistent part survives, with less noise.

Bias correction

Both averages start at 0. Dividing by undoes that exactly (next slide).

Defaults

(Kingma & Ba, 2015)

Explain

  • Line by line, starting from RMSProp: (1) add the first moment m, an EMA of g; (2) correct m and v for their zero start; (3) step along m̂ instead of g, divided by √v̂ instead of √v.
  • The mini-chart: a gradient that alternates ±2 around a small mean of 0.3. The bars swing, the bias-corrected m̂ (purple) settles near 0.3: momentum keeps the signal and averages away the flip.
  • Why β₂ = 0.999 is so much longer than β₁ = 0.9: the scale estimate should be stable (squared gradients are spiky), while the direction should stay responsive.

In your code

src/core/optimizers.py: Adam._update_moments is lines 1 and 2 plus the corrections; step() is the last line. It increments step_count before computing 1 − βᵗ, so t starts at 1 and the correction never divides by zero.

Check yourself

  • Which line would you delete to get back to (bias-corrected) RMSProp? The m line: use g in place of m̂.

08 · Adam · Bias correction

Why the correction is exactly 1/(1 − βᵗ)

Unroll the moving average. The weights on real gradients add up to ; the missing sits on the zero you started from.

1 · Unroll, with
2 · Take expectations, assuming for every step
3 · Geometric series
4 · Divide it out

Same for , with and .

Weights inside

β

Explain

  • Each update keeps β of the old m and adds (1−β) of the new gradient. Unrolled, gradient g_i ends up with weight (1−β)·β^(t−i): the newest has weight (1−β), the one before (1−β)β, and so on.
  • Those weights form a geometric series. Summed over the t real gradients they give 1 − βᵗ. The other βᵗ of the weight is on m₀ = 0, which pulls m toward zero.
  • If every gradient has the same expectation, E[m_t] = (1−βᵗ)·E[g]. Dividing by (1 − βᵗ) makes it unbiased. That is the whole derivation.
  • Drag t on the right: the grey "m₀ = 0" share shrinks as βᵗ. With β = 0.9 it is gone after a few dozen steps. With β = 0.999 (v's setting) it is still 96% at t = 40: v needs the correction for a long time.
  • At t = 1: m₁ = (1−β)g₁ and the correction multiplies by 1/(1−β), giving exactly g₁. The first step is exactly α·g₁/|g₁| = ±α.

Check yourself

  • Why is the correction for v much more important than for m? β₂ = 0.999 is closer to 1, so β₂ᵗ stays large for ~1,000s of steps; β₁ᵗ = 0.9ᵗ is negligible after ~40 steps.

08 · Adam · What the correction buys

Uncorrected, Adam's early steps are up to 6.6× too big

With a steady gradient, the uncorrected ratio is times the right size.

RMSProp at β = 0.999

31.6× at the first step, as on slide 19.

Adam, uncorrected

is also biased low, which partly cancels. But dies in ~20 steps and lasts ~1,000s: 3.2× at step 1, 6.6× at step 12, still 1.26× at step 1,000.

Adam, corrected

Exactly 1× from the first step. No warm-up needed just to undo the zero start.

Constant gradient, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε ignored. Step size in units of α.

Explain

  • With a constant gradient g: m_t = (1−β₁ᵗ)g and v_t = (1−β₂ᵗ)g². So m_t/√v_t = (1−β₁ᵗ)/√(1−β₂ᵗ) · sign(g).
  • At t = 1 that is 0.1/0.0316 = 3.16. Then m's bias disappears quickly but v's doesn't, so the ratio climbs to 6.6 around step 12 before slowly falling back.
  • Kingma & Ba show that without the correction, training with β₂ close to 1 can blow up early. Warm-up schedules are still common in practice, but for other reasons (v̂ rests on few samples early on).

Check yourself

  • Adam with β₁ = β₂ and no correction: how far off is the first step? (1−β)/√(1−β) = √(1−β): too small, not too big.

08 · Adam · Playground

All three on the valley

SGDRMSProp (β = 0.9)Adam (0.9, 0.999)same noise sequence for all three

No noise: Adam settles; its slow average still remembers the large early gradients, so its steps shrink. RMSProp's short window forgets them, so it bounces.

Turn noise up: SGD and RMSProp rattle around the minimum. Adam's momentum averages the noise, and it ends up lowest.

SGD
RMSProp
Adam

final loss, mean of the last 20 steps

Things to try

  • Noise 0, 200 steps: compare the three loss curves. SGD declines steadily; RMSProp plunges then bounces at ≈ ½(a+b)(η/2)²; Adam spirals in and keeps going down.
  • Noise 0.3: Adam ends more than 10× lower than the other two (with the default settings: about 0.004 vs 0.1 for RMSProp and 0.5 for SGD).
  • Raise a to 200 with noise on: SGD has to drop its learning rate below 0.01 and stalls; the adaptive methods barely notice.
  • Small step size (0.01) for the adaptive methods: they become slow but very smooth. The step size really is "distance per step".

Noise model

Each step's gradient is the true gradient plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation noise·(√a, √b), the same sequence for all three optimizers.

08 · Recap

Recap: each fix, and what it broke

METHOD
UPDATE
FIXES
STILL BREAKS
SGD
follows the slope
one η for all directions: the steepest sets it, the flattest crawls
Newton
a step per direction, from curvature
H has n² entries: unaffordable
Rprop
scale-free, immune to κ
minibatches: signs can't average noise away
AdaGrad
keeps magnitude; rare features keep big steps
the sum only grows: steps decay like 1/√t
RMSProp
tracks the recent scale; η becomes a distance
noisy direction, inflated first steps, jitter at the bottom
Adam
momentum + exact bias correction
needs decoupled weight decay (AdamW) and a schedule

Next

The companion deck Adam-optimizer.html covers Adam in practice: the two moments' jobs, AdamW, learning rates and warm-up, and memory cost.

Check yourself, across the deck

  • Why does SGD need about κ steps on the valley? η < 2/a for stability, so the flat direction shrinks by only 1 − 2/κ per step.
  • Rprop and RMSProp both normalise away the gradient's scale. What does RMSProp keep that Rprop throws away? The relative magnitudes of consecutive gradients, so noise can cancel.
  • AdaGrad vs RMSProp in one sentence? Sum of g² vs moving average of g²: a step size that only decays vs one that tracks the current scale.
  • What does η mean for RMSProp and Adam? Roughly how far each parameter moves per step, in its own units.
  • Where does 1/(1 − βᵗ) come from? The EMA's weights on real gradients sum to 1 − βᵗ; the rest sits on the zero initialisation.
